title: I started building a news app in my bedroom when I was a teenager.
body:
Most people told me the industry was already full. They said the big legacy players had won and that nobody wanted a new way to read the news. But I saw something different. I saw people overwhelmed by noise and struggling to find signal in a feed that was designed to keep them scrolling rather than informed.

Building Headlinne wasn't about disrupting an industry for the sake of it. It was about solving a personal frustration. I wanted a news experience that respected my time and actually tailored itself to what I cared about, rather than what an algorithm thought would keep me angry or distracted.

Being a young founder meant I had to learn the hard way. I had to figure out how to build AI that actually works, how to handle editorial integrity, and how to make technology feel human. It forced me to focus on the basics of good journalism and smart engineering. I stopped worrying about viral trends and started focusing on utility.

We are now at a point where AI can finally do what we were promised it would. It can act as a personal editor that cuts through the clutter, not just a content generator. The goal has always been simple: help people understand the world better without the headache.
cta: If you want to see what a cleaner, smarter way to read the news looks like, come take a look at HEADLINNE.com.
